module.title: Data, Math & Evaluation
module.subtitle: The part that decides whether the model is worth anything.
module.description: Models are downstream of data and metrics. Learn how to audit a dataset, build intuition for the math behind embeddings and gradients, and choose evaluation metrics that match the real cost of mistakes.
outcomes: Audit a tabular dataset for schema, missingness, duplicates and leakage.
Explain vectors, dot products, probability, loss and gradient descent in plain language.
Choose a metric and threshold from the cost of false positives and false negatives.

lessons.title: Data is the product
lessons.summary: A dataset audit that catches the failures models cannot fix later.
lessons.body_html:
A model cannot recover from a dataset that answers the wrong question. Before modelling, write a short data contract: what one row represents, what the target means, when each feature is known, and which rows are out of scope.

The first audit

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("customers.csv")
print(df.shape)
print(df.dtypes)
print(df.isna().mean().sort_values(ascending=False).head(10))
print("duplicate rows:", df.duplicated().sum())
print(df["churned"].value_counts(normalize=True))

Look for missing values, impossible ranges, duplicate IDs, inconsistent categories, and timestamps that reveal when data was recorded. Missingness itself can be a signal, but only if it is known at prediction time.

Leakage is a design bug

Leakage appears when a feature is created after the outcome. Examples: a cancellation reason when predicting cancellation, a refund flag when predicting fraud, or a customer segment assigned by a human after reviewing the case. The fix is not a better model; it is removing the field or reconstructing the data as it existed at decision time.

Split by time, not just randomly

If the product predicts next month from this month, a random split can put future rows in training. Use a temporal split: train on older data, validate on newer data. For grouped data (one customer, many rows), split by group so the same customer does not appear on both sides.

train = df[df["month"] < "2026-07"]
valid = df[df["month"] >= "2026-07"]

Privacy and provenance

Remove direct identifiers unless they are essential. Document where the data came from, who approved its use, how long you may keep it, and whether it contains personal or regulated information. A model trained on data you cannot legally use is a liability, not an asset.

Audit output: one page with row count, target rate, missingness, leakage risks, split strategy, and known limitations. This page is often more valuable than the model itself.
takeaways: Define what one row means and when each feature is known.
Leakage is usually a design bug, not a model bug.
Use temporal or grouped splits when the deployment setting requires them.
lessons.practice: Take a dataset you can access and write a one-page data contract: row meaning, target, prediction moment, missingness, split strategy and three leakage risks. Success: every field is labelled as known or unknown at prediction time.

lessons.title: The math you need, in pictures
lessons.summary: Vectors, dot products, probability, loss, and gradients — enough intuition to reason about models.
lessons.body_html:
You do not need to derive every equation to be an effective AI engineer. You do need to understand what the model is optimizing and why distance, probability, and gradients show up everywhere.

Vectors are points with meaning

A vector is an ordered list of numbers. An embedding is a vector where nearby points mean similar things. A 1,536-dimensional embedding is hard to visualize, but the geometry still works: similarity is often measured with a dot product or cosine similarity.

cosine(a, b) = (a · b) / (||a|| ||b||)

Cosine similarity ignores magnitude and compares direction. That is useful for text embeddings, where the length of a document should not dominate similarity.

Matrices are transformations

A matrix maps a vector to another vector. A neural network layer is essentially a learned matrix plus a bias and a non-linear activation. Matrix multiplication is how batches of examples move through the network efficiently.

Probability turns scores into decisions

A classifier often outputs a score. A sigmoid maps a score to a probability between 0 and 1. A threshold turns that probability into a label. The threshold is a product decision: lowering it catches more positives but creates more false alarms.

Loss is the thing being minimized

Cross-entropy penalizes confident wrong answers. Mean squared error penalizes distance for regression. The optimizer changes parameters to reduce the loss on training data, while validation data tells you whether that progress generalizes.

Gradient descent in one sentence

A gradient points uphill; the optimizer steps downhill. The learning rate controls the step size. Too large and training diverges; too small and it crawls.

parameters ← parameters - learning_rate × gradient

Backpropagation is the efficient way to compute those gradients through a network. You will use frameworks that do it for you, but knowing the shape of the idea helps you debug exploding losses and silent non-learning.

Intuition check: if someone asks why two embeddings are similar, you should be able to say “their directions align, measured by cosine similarity” without reaching for a research paper.
takeaways: Embeddings are vectors; cosine similarity compares their direction.
A neural network layer is a learned matrix plus a non-linearity.
Loss defines what the model optimizes; the gradient points toward worse loss.
lessons.practice: Explain cosine similarity, loss and gradient descent to a non-ML friend in 150 words. Success: no unexplained jargon, and you can give one example of each.

lessons.title: Metrics that match the decision
lessons.summary: Accuracy is a starting point, not a decision. Learn precision, recall, PR-AUC, calibration, and regression errors.
lessons.body_html:
Every metric encodes a value judgment. Choose it by asking what a false positive costs, what a false negative costs, and what volume of alerts a human can actually handle.

The confusion matrix

                 predicted positive   predicted negative
actual positive       true positive        false negative
actual negative       false positive       true negative

Precision = TP / (TP + FP): when the model says positive, how often is it right? Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of all real positives, how many did it catch? F1 balances the two when both matter.

Thresholds and ranking

Most classifiers output a score. ROC-AUC measures ranking across all thresholds; PR-AUC is often more informative when positives are rare. Neither tells you the exact threshold to ship. Pick the threshold from the cost of errors and the capacity of the downstream process.

from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, precision_recall_curve

print(classification_report(y_test, pred))
precision, recall, thresholds = precision_recall_curve(y_test, scores)

Calibration

A model is calibrated when a predicted 0.8 really means roughly 80% positive. Tree ensembles can be miscalibrated. If a human uses the probability directly, calibration matters as much as ranking.

Regression metrics

  • MAE — average absolute error, easy to explain in the target unit.
  • RMSE — penalizes large errors more heavily.
  • MAPE — percentage error, unstable when the true value is near zero.

Report a baseline and a slice analysis. Overall RMSE can hide a model that is excellent for large customers and useless for new ones.

Metric brief: write one sentence for each error type — what happens to the user, the business, and the system — then choose the metric and threshold. “High accuracy” is not a metric brief.
takeaways: Every metric encodes a value judgment about false positives and false negatives.
Precision and recall describe different failures; thresholds turn scores into decisions.
Calibration and slice analysis matter when the number drives a real action.
lessons.practice: For a fraud detector, write the cost of a false positive and a false negative, choose a metric and a threshold, and name one customer slice you would inspect. Success: another person can defend the decision from your note.

lessons.title: Applied deep dive: a churn audit from CSV to memo
lessons.summary: A complete, reproducible audit: schema, leakage, temporal split, baseline, metrics and the decision memo.
lessons.body_html:
A churn audit is a decision document disguised as an analysis. The model is only one paragraph; the split, metric and limitations are the rest.

1. State the prediction moment

Example: On the first day of each month, predict whether a customer will cancel before the next billing date, using only data available on that day. Every feature must pass that test.

2. Audit the frame

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("customer_months.csv")
print(df.shape)
print(df.dtypes)
print(df.isna().mean().sort_values(ascending=False).head(10))
print(df.duplicated(subset=["customer_id", "month"]).sum())
print(df["churned"].value_counts(normalize=True))

Look for duplicate customer-months, missing labels, impossible values and features recorded after cancellation.

3. Split by time

train = df[df["month"] < "2026-07"].copy()
valid = df[df["month"] >= "2026-07"].copy()
print(train["month"].max(), valid["month"].min())

If the product predicts next month, a random split can train on the future. Check the boundary and the label rate in both splits.

4. Baseline, then model

from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

baseline = DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent").fit(train[features], train["churned"])
model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(train[features], train["churned"])

for name, estimator in [("baseline", baseline), ("logistic", model)]:
    pred = estimator.predict(valid[features])
    print(name)
    print(classification_report(valid["churned"], pred, zero_division=0))

The baseline tells you whether the model learned anything. The report shows whether the model is useful for the actual decision.

5. Choose a threshold and write the memo

Suppose a retention offer costs 10 and saves 80 of future revenue. A false positive wastes 10; a false negative loses 80. Choose the threshold that reflects that ratio, then report precision and recall at that threshold. The memo should contain:

  • decision and prediction moment;
  • row counts, label rate and split dates;
  • leakage risks removed or unresolved;
  • baseline and model metrics at the chosen threshold;
  • slices (plan, tenure) and one explicit limitation.
Interview story: “We did not ship the model because the baseline was already strong at the campaign capacity” is a valid, senior-sounding result.
takeaways: The prediction moment determines which features are legal.
A temporal split is part of the problem definition, not a preprocessing detail.
The audit memo is the deliverable; the model supports it.
lessons.practice: Write the prediction moment, list three leakage risks and choose a cost-based threshold. Success: a reviewer can reproduce your split and explain the threshold without asking you.

lessons.title: Probability, uncertainty and calibration
lessons.summary: What a model score really means, and why confidence must be measured rather than assumed.
lessons.body_html:
A model that says “0.9” is making a claim about the world. Calibration asks whether that claim is true: among all cases scored around 0.9, roughly 90% should be positive.

Where uncertainty comes from

  • Aleatoric uncertainty — irreducible noise in the data.
  • Epistemic uncertainty — the model does not know because it has not seen enough relevant data.
  • Distribution shift — the input no longer resembles training data.

A single softmax probability often hides all three. That is why out-of-distribution detection and abstention are separate problems.

Measure calibration

import numpy as np
from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve

prob_true, prob_pred = calibration_curve(
    y_valid, scores, n_bins=10, strategy="quantile"
)
# Points near the diagonal mean the probabilities are trustworthy.

Brier score combines calibration and discrimination. A model can rank well but be badly calibrated; if a human uses the number directly, that matters.

Thresholds are not probabilities

threshold = 0.35
prediction = scores >= threshold

Lowering the threshold increases recall and false positives. The threshold is a product decision; the probability is a model output. Keep them separate in code and documentation.

When to abstain

Abstain when confidence is low, the input is out of distribution, or the evidence is insufficient. Measure coverage — the fraction of cases the system handles — alongside accuracy on the covered set. A model that answers 60% of cases with 95% accuracy may be more useful than one that answers everything with 70%.

Debugging check: if predicted probabilities are all near 0.5, the model may be underfit, badly scaled or trained on contradictory labels.
takeaways: Calibration measures whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies.
A ranking score and a deployment threshold are different objects.
Abstention and coverage are product features, not model failures.
lessons.practice: Plot a calibration curve for any classifier and compare it with a threshold-based decision. Success: you can explain whether a human should trust the number or only the ranking.

questions.prompt: What does one row in a training table usually represent?
choices: One model parameter.
One example or entity at a specific point in time.
One evaluation metric.
One API request.
questions.explanation: The row is the unit of learning. Defining it precisely (customer-month, order, session) prevents double counting, leakage, and ambiguous labels.

questions.prompt: Why is a temporal split often better than a random split for product data?
choices: It makes the dataset smaller.
It mimics predicting the future from the past and reduces leakage.
It guarantees a higher accuracy.
It removes the need for a baseline.
questions.explanation: A random split can put future information in training. A time-based split better matches the deployment setting: train on the past, evaluate on later data.

questions.prompt: A feature has 40% missing values. What is the best first step?
choices: Fill every missing value with zero.
Understand why it is missing and whether missingness is known at prediction time.
Drop the column immediately.
Ignore it; tree models handle everything.
questions.explanation: Missingness can be informative or can encode leakage. Understand the mechanism before choosing imputation, a missing indicator, or removal.

questions.prompt: What does a cosine similarity of 0.95 between two text embeddings mean?
choices: The texts are exactly identical.
Their embedding directions are very similar, which usually suggests semantic similarity.
The texts have 95 words in common.
The model is 95% accurate.
questions.explanation: Cosine measures the angle between vectors, not exact equality. High similarity often means related meaning, but it must be validated for your model and domain.

questions.prompt: A fraud model has high ROC-AUC but the team still misses most fraud. What is a likely explanation?
choices: ROC-AUC is always wrong.
The operating threshold is too high for the recall the team needs, or the class imbalance makes ROC-AUC look better than the deployed precision/recall trade-off.
The model needs more layers.
The test set was too large.
questions.explanation: ROC-AUC summarizes ranking across thresholds, not the threshold you chose. Inspect the precision-recall curve at the operating point and the cost of missed fraud.

questions.prompt: When is a model's calibration more important than its ranking?
choices: When the model only ranks items and no human sees the score.
When a human or another system uses the predicted probability as a real probability, for example to price risk or decide whether to escalate.
When the dataset is small.
When using a random forest.
questions.explanation: Ranking only needs order. Calibration matters when the numeric probability drives a decision: expected loss, pricing, triage, or an automatic threshold.

flashcards.back: Information in training that will not be available at prediction time, or that is derived from the target. It creates optimistic offline scores and poor production behavior.
Precision: of the predicted positives, how many were correct. Recall: of the actual positives, how many were found. The right balance depends on the cost of false alarms versus misses.
It mimics the real deployment setting: train on older data, evaluate on newer data. It also prevents future rows from leaking into training.
The cosine of the angle between two vectors. It compares direction rather than magnitude, which is useful for text embeddings.
Calibration means predicted probabilities match observed frequencies: among cases scored 0.8, about 80% should be positive. It matters when the number itself drives a decision.
